articles.title: Moving to Ireland from Austria
articles.note: EU free movement, no visa or permit, licence valid as is, tax treaty, pension agreement.

articles.previewHtml:
Austria sends a steady trickle of people to Ireland rather than a flood, most of them arriving for jobs in tech, pharma, finance and engineering, or for a year or two of English-language study and university exchange. Many come because an Irish office of an international employer offered a role that suited them, and stay because the work culture feels more relaxed than expected. Others follow an Irish partner home after meeting them abroad. The thing that most surprises Austrians is how informal Irish workplaces are, with first names for everyone and very little ceremony.

Quick factsAustria to Ireland
Visa to enterNo: EU free movement
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysNo permit or registration needed
Austrian licence exchangeableDrive on it, swap it when it expires
Double taxation agreementYes
Social security agreementYes, via EU rules
PetsEU pet passport

Do you need a visa?

No. As an EU citizen you have the right to free movement: you can enter Ireland with a passport or national identity card, look for work, take a job, study or set up a business without a visa, an employment permit or any registration with immigration. There is no Irish Residence Permit for EU, EEA and Swiss citizens. After three months you are expected to be working, self-employed, studying, or able to support yourself, but nobody checks at a desk; it only comes up if you later apply for something like citizenship.

The picture changes for family. A spouse, partner or dependent parent who is not an EU, EEA or Swiss citizen can join you under EU Treaty Rights: they may need a visa to enter, and once here they apply to Immigration Service Delivery for a residence card (form EU1) within their first months, which gives them Stamp 4 EU FAM and the right to work. Applying early matters because the card can take months.

If you have an Irish parent or grandparent you may already be entitled to Irish citizenship through the Foreign Births Register. It changes nothing about your right to live here, but an Irish passport is handy for family members and for voting.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

Most Austrians arrive with strong school English and a good ear, though Irish accents and speed of speech can take a few weeks to tune into. Employers will judge you on the interview rather than a certificate, while universities and professional bodies may still ask for a formal test. Irish appears on signs, but nobody expects you to speak it.

You can apply for jobs from home and start the week you land. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites, with recruitment agencies strong in tech, finance and pharma. EU qualifications are recognised under EU rules, so a nurse, doctor, teacher or engineer registers with the Irish body without re-qualifying, though registration itself takes weeks to months.

Your driving licence

A full Austrian licence is an EU or EEA licence, so you can keep driving on it in Ireland for as long as it is valid; there is no exchange deadline. Most people swap it for an Irish licence when it expires or when they want a local card for identification, which the NDLS does without a test for 65 euro. Apply online at ndls.ie with a Public Services Card and MyGovID, or book an NDLS centre appointment with the licence, proof of your PPS number, proof of address and photo ID. Once you exchange it, Irish rules apply: a lifetime licence becomes a ten year one, and category B does not include the trailers or motorcycles it may have covered at home.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Austria have a double taxation agreement, so income taxed in one country is generally credited in the other and the treaty decides which country taxes what. You become Irish tax resident after 183 days in a tax year (or 280 days over two years), and from then Ireland taxes your worldwide income, with credit for Austrian tax under the treaty. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number so your employer taxes you correctly, and tell the Austrian tax authority that you are leaving.

Social security follows the EU coordination rules. You pay into one system at a time, your Austrian contribution record and Irish PRSI record are combined to qualify for a state pension in either country, and each country pays its share when you retire. If your employer is posting you to Ireland temporarily, an A1 certificate keeps you in the Austrian system. Occupational and private pensions can generally stay where they are.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Being in the euro area spares you exchange costs, and SEPA transfers from home arrive the next day.

Healthcare

Your European Health Insurance Card covers you as a visitor, not as a resident. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. The HSE is not free at the point of use the way many Austrian services are: a GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 and people over 70 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. If your employer is posting you here on an A1, an S1 form registers you with the HSE at Austrian expense.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods move freely inside the EU, so a removals van from Austria clears no customs. A car registered in Austria must be registered for Vehicle Registration Tax within 30 days of arrival; VRT relief applies if you owned and used the car for at least 6 months abroad and are moving your normal residence to Ireland, and you then need Irish insurance, motor tax and an NCT.

Pets travel on an EU pet passport: a microchip, a rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel, and for dogs a tapeworm treatment by a vet 24 to 120 hours before arrival, which Ireland requires because it is free of the tapeworm. Ferries and airlines carry pets on set routes, and the animal is checked on arrival.

Settling in: community and daily life

The Austrian community in Ireland is small and mostly professional, concentrated in Dublin with a scattering in Cork and Galway. Newcomers tend to find each other through the embassy's cultural events, German-speaking Facebook and WhatsApp groups, Stammtisch meetups and the wider German-speaking circles that Austrians, Germans and Swiss share.

You will miss the mountains and the crisp winters, and the grey mild dampness takes getting used to. Renting is less regulated and more competitive than at home, and you will rarely see a rental contract that lasts as long as an Austrian one. Cards are accepted almost everywhere, shops open late and on Sundays, and pubs replace the Kaffeehaus as the place where social life happens.

Getting home is straightforward: there are direct flights between Dublin and Austria, and Cork and Shannon add more routes in summer.

First 30 days checklist

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • No IRP is needed. Register with Revenue myAccount once you have a PPS number so your employer can tax you correctly.
  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.
  • Get a Leap card for public transport; your licence needs nothing until it expires.

★ Useful links

  • Immigration Service Delivery: family members of EU citizens
  • National Driver Licence Service
  • Revenue: moving to Ireland
  • Bilateral social security agreements and EU rules
  • Department of Agriculture: bringing your pet to Ireland
  • Health Insurance Authority

Bulgarians arrive for roles in tech support and software, construction, hospitality, healthcare, logistics and manufacturing, and increasingly for university places. Double taxation agreementYes
Social security agreementYes, via EU rules

articles.previewHtml:
Luxembourg is a small country whose people are used to working in several languages across borders, so Luxembourgers fit naturally into Dublin's finance, funds, tech and EU-facing consultancy jobs. Some move on internal transfers within international firms, others for Irish universities or for a partner, and a few because they want a bigger, English-speaking city with a similar open economy. The thing that most surprises Luxembourgers is how informal and chatty Irish workplaces are, and how quickly colleagues become friends over a pint.

Quick factsLuxembourg to Ireland
Visa to enterNo: EU free movement
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysNo permit or registration needed
Luxembourgish licence exchangeableDrive on it, swap it when it expires
Double taxation agreementYes
Social security agreementYes, via EU rules
PetsEU pet passport

Do you need a visa?

No. As an EU citizen you have the right to free movement: you can enter Ireland with a passport or national identity card, look for work, take a job, study or set up a business without a visa, an employment permit or any registration with immigration. There is no Irish Residence Permit for EU, EEA and Swiss citizens. After three months you are expected to be working, self-employed, studying, or able to support yourself, but nobody checks at a desk; it only comes up if you later apply for something like citizenship.

The picture changes for family. A spouse, partner or dependent parent who is not an EU, EEA or Swiss citizen can join you under EU Treaty Rights: they may need a visa to enter, and once here they apply to Immigration Service Delivery for a residence card (form EU1) within their first months, which gives them Stamp 4 EU FAM and the right to work. Applying early matters because the card can take months.

If you have an Irish parent or grandparent you may already be entitled to Irish citizenship through the Foreign Births Register. It changes nothing about your right to live here, but an Irish passport is handy for family members and for voting.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

Luxembourgers usually arrive with fluent English on top of Luxembourgish, French and German, and settle into Irish workplaces easily. Employers hire on the interview, while universities and professional bodies may ask for a formal test. Irish is on signs but is never needed.

You can apply for jobs from home and start the week you land. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites, with recruitment agencies strong in tech, finance and pharma. EU qualifications are recognised under EU rules, so a nurse, doctor, teacher or engineer registers with the Irish body without re-qualifying, though registration itself takes weeks to months.

Your driving licence

A full Luxembourgish licence is an EU or EEA licence, so you can keep driving on it in Ireland for as long as it is valid; there is no exchange deadline. Most people swap it for an Irish licence when it expires or when they want a local card for identification, which the NDLS does without a test for 65 euro. Apply online at ndls.ie with a Public Services Card and MyGovID, or book an NDLS centre appointment with the licence, proof of your PPS number, proof of address and photo ID. Once you exchange it, Irish rules apply: a lifetime licence becomes a ten year one, and category B does not include the trailers or motorcycles it may have covered at home.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Luxembourg have a double taxation agreement, so income taxed in one country is generally credited in the other and the treaty decides which country taxes what. You become Irish tax resident after 183 days in a tax year (or 280 days over two years), and from then Ireland taxes your worldwide income, with credit for Luxembourgish tax under the treaty. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number so your employer taxes you correctly, and tell the Luxembourgish tax authority that you are leaving.

Social security follows the EU coordination rules. You pay into one system at a time, your Luxembourgish contribution record and Irish PRSI record are combined to qualify for a state pension in either country, and each country pays its share when you retire. If your employer is posting you to Ireland temporarily, an A1 certificate keeps you in the Luxembourgish system. Occupational and private pensions can generally stay where they are.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Being in the euro area spares you exchange costs, and SEPA transfers from home arrive the next day.

Healthcare

Your European Health Insurance Card covers you as a visitor, not as a resident. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. The HSE is not free at the point of use the way many Luxembourgish services are: a GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 and people over 70 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. If your employer is posting you here on an A1, an S1 form registers you with the HSE at Luxembourgish expense.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods move freely inside the EU, so a removals van from Luxembourg clears no customs. A car registered in Luxembourg must be registered for Vehicle Registration Tax within 30 days of arrival; VRT relief applies if you owned and used the car for at least 6 months abroad and are moving your normal residence to Ireland, and you then need Irish insurance, motor tax and an NCT.

Pets travel on an EU pet passport: a microchip, a rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel, and for dogs a tapeworm treatment by a vet 24 to 120 hours before arrival, which Ireland requires because it is free of the tapeworm. Ferries and airlines carry pets on set routes, and the animal is checked on arrival.

Settling in: community and daily life

Luxembourgers in Ireland are a very small community, mostly professionals in Dublin, and they usually join the larger francophone, German-speaking and Belgian circles rather than forming their own. People meet through embassy and honorary consulate events, EU-related networks, Facebook groups and the shared gatherings of neighbouring countries.

The climate is similar but windier and wetter than at home, with fewer cold snaps and less snow. Renting is expensive and less regulated, and groceries and eating out cost more than in Luxembourg, though wages in similar sectors are comparable. Cards are used everywhere, public transport is not free, shops open on Sundays and social life revolves around the pub.

Getting home is straightforward: there are direct flights between Dublin and Luxembourg, and Cork and Shannon add more routes in summer.

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • No IRP is needed. Register with Revenue myAccount once you have a PPS number so your employer can tax you correctly.
  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.
  • Get a Leap card for public transport; your licence needs nothing until it expires.

The Netherlands and Ireland are close neighbours by air and trade, and Dutch people move to Ireland for jobs in tech, finance, aviation leasing, pharma, agriculture and consultancy, for Irish universities and research, or for a partner. Many arrive through international employers who want Dutch speakers in Dublin, and others come for the slower pace and the coastline of the west. The thing that most surprises the Dutch is how indirect Irish communication is, with no blunt no and plenty of reading between the lines.

Quick factsThe Netherlands to Ireland
Visa to enterNo: EU free movement
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysNo permit or registration needed
Dutch licence exchangeableDrive on it, swap it when it expires
Double taxation agreementYes
Social security agreementYes, via EU rules
PetsEU pet passport

Do you need a visa?

No. As an EU citizen you have the right to free movement: you can enter Ireland with a passport or national identity card, look for work, take a job, study or set up a business without a visa, an employment permit or any registration with immigration. There is no Irish Residence Permit for EU, EEA and Swiss citizens. After three months you are expected to be working, self-employed, studying, or able to support yourself, but nobody checks at a desk; it only comes up if you later apply for something like citizenship.

The picture changes for family. A spouse, partner or dependent parent who is not an EU, EEA or Swiss citizen can join you under EU Treaty Rights: they may need a visa to enter, and once here they apply to Immigration Service Delivery for a residence card (form EU1) within their first months, which gives them Stamp 4 EU FAM and the right to work. Applying early matters because the card can take months.

If you have an Irish parent or grandparent you may already be entitled to Irish citizenship through the Foreign Births Register. It changes nothing about your right to live here, but an Irish passport is handy for family members and for voting.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

Dutch people arrive with near-fluent English and slot into Irish workplaces without difficulty, though Irish directness runs the other way from Dutch directness and can take time to read. Employers hire on the interview, while universities and professional bodies may ask for a test. Irish is on signs but is never needed.

You can apply for jobs from home and start the week you land. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites, with recruitment agencies strong in tech, finance and pharma. EU qualifications are recognised under EU rules, so a nurse, doctor, teacher or engineer registers with the Irish body without re-qualifying, though registration itself takes weeks to months.

Your driving licence

A full Dutch licence is an EU or EEA licence, so you can keep driving on it in Ireland for as long as it is valid; there is no exchange deadline. Most people swap it for an Irish licence when it expires or when they want a local card for identification, which the NDLS does without a test for 65 euro. Apply online at ndls.ie with a Public Services Card and MyGovID, or book an NDLS centre appointment with the licence, proof of your PPS number, proof of address and photo ID. Once you exchange it, Irish rules apply: a lifetime licence becomes a ten year one, and category B does not include the trailers or motorcycles it may have covered at home.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and the Netherlands have a double taxation agreement, so income taxed in one country is generally credited in the other and the treaty decides which country taxes what. You become Irish tax resident after 183 days in a tax year (or 280 days over two years), and from then Ireland taxes your worldwide income, with credit for Dutch tax under the treaty. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number so your employer taxes you correctly, and tell the Dutch tax authority that you are leaving.

Social security follows the EU coordination rules. You pay into one system at a time, your Dutch contribution record and Irish PRSI record are combined to qualify for a state pension in either country, and each country pays its share when you retire. If your employer is posting you to Ireland temporarily, an A1 certificate keeps you in the Dutch system. Occupational and private pensions can generally stay where they are.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Being in the euro area spares you exchange costs, and SEPA transfers from home arrive the next day.

Healthcare

Your European Health Insurance Card covers you as a visitor, not as a resident. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. The HSE is not free at the point of use the way many Dutch services are: a GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 and people over 70 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. If your employer is posting you here on an A1, an S1 form registers you with the HSE at Dutch expense.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods move freely inside the EU, so a removals van from the Netherlands clears no customs. A car registered in the Netherlands must be registered for Vehicle Registration Tax within 30 days of arrival; VRT relief applies if you owned and used the car for at least 6 months abroad and are moving your normal residence to Ireland, and you then need Irish insurance, motor tax and an NCT.

Pets travel on an EU pet passport: a microchip, a rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel, and for dogs a tapeworm treatment by a vet 24 to 120 hours before arrival, which Ireland requires because it is free of the tapeworm. Ferries and airlines carry pets on set routes, and the animal is checked on arrival.

Settling in: community and daily life

The Dutch community in Ireland is medium-sized and well established, mostly in Dublin with groups in Cork, Galway and rural areas where Dutch farmers settled. Newcomers find each other through Dutch Facebook and WhatsApp groups, Koningsdag and Sinterklaas events, the Dutch church and school activities, embassy events and hockey and football clubs.

The climate is similar but wetter, windier and hillier, and cycling is far less easy and safe than at home. Renting is expensive and leases are short, and the cost of groceries and eating out is higher. Cards are used everywhere, cars drive on the left, shops open on Sundays, and the pub is the social venue rather than a borrel at home or the office.

Getting home is straightforward: there are direct flights between Dublin and the Netherlands, and Cork and Shannon add more routes in summer.

First 30 days checklist

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • No IRP is needed. Register with Revenue myAccount once you have a PPS number so your employer can tax you correctly.
  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.
  • Get a Leap card for public transport; your licence needs nothing until it expires.

  • Immigration Service Delivery: family members of EU citizens
  • National Driver Licence Service
  • Revenue: moving to Ireland
  • Bilateral social security agreements and EU rules
  • Department of Agriculture: bringing your pet to Ireland
  • Health Insurance Authority

articles.plainText:
Sweden sends a small but steady stream of people to Ireland for work in tech, gaming, pharma, finance and telecoms, for research and degrees at Irish universities, and quite often for a partner. Some come for the music, the coastline and a friendlier, less structured working culture than at home. Ireland's English-speaking workplaces make the transfer simple within international firms. The thing that most surprises Swedes is how spontaneous and unplanned Irish social life is, with plans made on the day and evenings that run far later than intended.

Do you need a visa?

No. As an EU citizen you have the right to free movement: you can enter Ireland with a passport or national identity card, look for work, take a job, study or set up a business without a visa, an employment permit or any registration with immigration. There is no Irish Residence Permit for EU, EEA and Swiss citizens. After three months you are expected to be working, self-employed, studying, or able to support yourself, but nobody checks at a desk; it only comes up if you later apply for something like citizenship.

The picture changes for family. A spouse, partner or dependent parent who is not an EU, EEA or Swiss citizen can join you under EU Treaty Rights: they may need a visa to enter, and once here they apply to Immigration Service Delivery for a residence card (form EU1) within their first months, which gives them Stamp 4 EU FAM and the right to work. Applying early matters because the card can take months.

If you have an Irish parent or grandparent you may already be entitled to Irish citizenship through the Foreign Births Register. It changes nothing about your right to live here, but an Irish passport is handy for family members and for voting.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

Swedes almost always arrive with fluent English and adapt quickly, though the Irish habit of chat and indirect answers can take a while to read. Employers hire on the interview, while universities and professional bodies may ask for a formal test. Irish appears on signs but is never needed.

You can apply for jobs from home and start the week you land. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites, with recruitment agencies strong in tech, finance and pharma. EU qualifications are recognised under EU rules, so a nurse, doctor, teacher or engineer registers with the Irish body without re-qualifying, though registration itself takes weeks to months.

Your driving licence

A full Swedish licence is an EU or EEA licence, so you can keep driving on it in Ireland for as long as it is valid; there is no exchange deadline. Most people swap it for an Irish licence when it expires or when they want a local card for identification, which the NDLS does without a test for 65 euro. Apply online at ndls.ie with a Public Services Card and MyGovID, or book an NDLS centre appointment with the licence, proof of your PPS number, proof of address and photo ID. Once you exchange it, Irish rules apply: a lifetime licence becomes a ten year one, and category B does not include the trailers or motorcycles it may have covered at home.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Sweden have a double taxation agreement, so income taxed in one country is generally credited in the other and the treaty decides which country taxes what. You become Irish tax resident after 183 days in a tax year (or 280 days over two years), and from then Ireland taxes your worldwide income, with credit for Swedish tax under the treaty. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number so your employer taxes you correctly, and tell the Swedish tax authority that you are leaving.

Social security follows the EU coordination rules. You pay into one system at a time, your Swedish contribution record and Irish PRSI record are combined to qualify for a state pension in either country, and each country pays its share when you retire. If your employer is posting you to Ireland temporarily, an A1 certificate keeps you in the Swedish system. Occupational and private pensions can generally stay where they are.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the Swedish krona into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Healthcare

Your European Health Insurance Card covers you as a visitor, not as a resident. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. The HSE is not free at the point of use the way many Swedish services are: a GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 and people over 70 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. If your employer is posting you here on an A1, an S1 form registers you with the HSE at Swedish expense.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods move freely inside the EU, so a removals van from Sweden clears no customs. A car registered in Sweden must be registered for Vehicle Registration Tax within 30 days of arrival; VRT relief applies if you owned and used the car for at least 6 months abroad and are moving your normal residence to Ireland, and you then need Irish insurance, motor tax and an NCT.

Pets travel on an EU pet passport: a microchip, a rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel, and for dogs a tapeworm treatment by a vet 24 to 120 hours before arrival, which Ireland requires because it is free of the tapeworm. Ferries and airlines carry pets on set routes, and the animal is checked on arrival.

Settling in: community and daily life

The Swedish community in Ireland is small and mostly professional, centred on Dublin with a few in Cork and Galway. People meet through the Swedish church's Lucia and Midsummer events, the embassy's national day reception, Nordic Facebook and WhatsApp groups and the shared Scandinavian meetups with Danes, Norwegians and Finns.

Winters are much milder and greener than Sweden's but still dark and grey, with far less snow and no long summer light. Renting is expensive and leases are short, and Irish houses can feel cold and damp compared with Swedish homes. Cards are used everywhere, alcohol is sold freely in shops and pubs, and social life happens in pubs rather than at home over fika.

Getting home is straightforward: there are direct flights between Dublin and Sweden, and Cork and Shannon add more routes in summer.

articles.title: Moving to Ireland from Albania
articles.note: D visa and a permit, no licence exchange, tax treaty, no pension agreement.
articles.description: Albania sends a steady trickle of people to Ireland rather than a flood, and most come for work in construction, hospitality, care and, increasingly, tech…
articles.previewHtml:
Albania sends a steady trickle of people to Ireland rather than a flood, and most come for work in construction, hospitality, care and, increasingly, tech and pharma. Younger Albanians often arrive for English-language study or a postgraduate course and then stay on for a job. Others follow family already settled in Dublin. What surprises many new arrivals is how soft and changeable the weather is: there is rarely a hard winter, but there is rarely a proper summer either, and rain can arrive on any day of the year.

Quick factsAlbania to Ireland
Visa to enterYes, long stay D visa
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Albanian licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementYes
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Albanian citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Albania, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

English is widely taught in Albania and many arrivals speak it well, though Irish accents take adjusting to. Employers rarely ask for a formal test, but universities and professional registration bodies usually do. Irish appears on signs but you will not need it.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Albanian qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Albania is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Albanian licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Albanian licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Albania have a double taxation agreement, so income taxed in one country is generally credited in the other and the treaty decides which country taxes what. You become Irish tax resident after 183 days in a tax year (or 280 days over two years), and from then Ireland taxes your worldwide income, with credit for Albanian tax under the treaty. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number so your employer taxes you correctly, and tell the Albanian tax authority that you are leaving.

There is no social security agreement between Ireland and Albania, so the two records stand alone. You need at least 520 paid PRSI contributions (ten years) to qualify for any Irish State Pension (Contributory), and the full rate takes 40 years of contributions. Check whether your Albanian state pension can be paid to you in Ireland, and whether you can keep contributing voluntarily from abroad.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the lek into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Healthcare

Ireland has a public system run by the HSE, but it is not free at the point of use. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods arriving from Albania are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year. A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from Albania rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.

Albania is an unlisted country under the EU pet rules, which adds a blood test. Your dog, cat or ferret needs a microchip, then a rabies vaccination, then a rabies antibody titre test at least 30 days after the vaccination at an EU approved laboratory, and then a three month wait from the date of the blood sample before travel. Add an EU animal health certificate issued within 10 days of travel and, for dogs, a tapeworm treatment 24 to 120 hours before arrival. Pets must arrive as manifest cargo or with an approved airline on an approved route (Dublin Airport handles most). Start the process at least four months before you fly.

Settling in: community and daily life

The Albanian community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, concentrated mostly in Dublin with smaller pockets around Cork and Limerick. Newcomers tend to find each other through Facebook and WhatsApp groups, a few cultural associations, and word of mouth among families who have been here a while.

You will notice the early nights first: shops and cafés close far earlier than in Tirana, and evening life happens in the pub rather than on the street. Card payments are accepted almost everywhere, tipping is modest and optional, and eating out costs noticeably more than at home. Driving is on the left, which takes a few weeks to feel natural.

There are no regular direct flights between Dublin and Albania, so getting home usually means one stop, most often via London, Frankfurt, Vienna, Istanbul or Warsaw; budget for the time as well as the fare.

First 30 days checklist

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • Register for your Irish Residence Permit within 90 days (300 euro); book the appointment the week you land because slots fill up.
  • Register with Revenue myAccount once you have a PPS number so your employer can tax you correctly.
  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.

Albania sends a steady trickle of people to Ireland rather than a flood, and most come for work in construction, hospitality, care and, increasingly, tech and pharma. Younger Albanians often arrive for English-language study or a postgraduate course and then stay on for a job. Others follow family already settled in Dublin. What surprises many new arrivals is how soft and changeable the weather is: there is rarely a hard winter, but there is rarely a proper summer either, and rain can arrive on any day of the year.

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Albanian citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Albania, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

English is widely taught in Albania and many arrivals speak it well, though Irish accents take adjusting to. Employers rarely ask for a formal test, but universities and professional registration bodies usually do. Irish appears on signs but you will not need it.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Albanian qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Albania is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Albanian licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Albanian licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Albania have a double taxation agreement, so income taxed in one country is generally credited in the other and the treaty decides which country taxes what. You become Irish tax resident after 183 days in a tax year (or 280 days over two years), and from then Ireland taxes your worldwide income, with credit for Albanian tax under the treaty. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number so your employer taxes you correctly, and tell the Albanian tax authority that you are leaving.

There is no social security agreement between Ireland and Albania, so the two records stand alone. You need at least 520 paid PRSI contributions (ten years) to qualify for any Irish State Pension (Contributory), and the full rate takes 40 years of contributions. Moving money from the lek into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Card payments are accepted almost everywhere, tipping is modest and optional, and eating out costs noticeably more than at home. Driving is on the left, which takes a few weeks to feel natural.

articles.previewHtml:
Bosnia and Herzegovina has a long habit of sending people abroad for work, and Ireland has become one of the destinations for engineers, healthcare workers, tradespeople and hospitality staff, alongside a growing number in tech and pharma. Some come for postgraduate study or English, others follow relatives already here, and the reason is usually ordinary: better pay, more opportunity, a change of scene. What surprises many Bosnians is the cost of a simple coffee and a night out compared with Sarajevo or Mostar, and how early everything closes.

Quick factsBosnia and Herzegovina to Ireland
Visa to enterYes, long stay D visa
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Bosnian licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementYes
Social security agreementNo
PetsListed country, no blood test

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Bosnian citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Bosnia and Herzegovina, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

Younger Bosnians often arrive with good English from school and television, while others build it on the job. Employers rarely ask for a test certificate, but universities and professional registration bodies will. Irish is on road signs and documents but you do not need it.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Bosnian qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Bosnia and Herzegovina is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Bosnian licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Bosnian licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Bosnia and Herzegovina have a double taxation agreement, so income taxed in one country is generally credited in the other and the treaty decides which country taxes what. You become Irish tax resident after 183 days in a tax year (or 280 days over two years), and from then Ireland taxes your worldwide income, with credit for Bosnian tax under the treaty. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number so your employer taxes you correctly, and tell the Bosnian tax authority that you are leaving.

There is no social security agreement between Ireland and Bosnia and Herzegovina, so the two records stand alone. You need at least 520 paid PRSI contributions (ten years) to qualify for any Irish State Pension (Contributory), and the full rate takes 40 years of contributions. Check whether your Bosnian state pension can be paid to you in Ireland, and whether you can keep contributing voluntarily from abroad.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the convertible mark into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Healthcare

Ireland has a public system run by the HSE, but it is not free at the point of use. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods arriving from Bosnia and Herzegovina are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year. A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from Bosnia and Herzegovina rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.

Bosnia and Herzegovina is a listed country under the EU pet rules, so no rabies blood test is needed. Your dog, cat or ferret needs a microchip, a rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel, an EU animal health certificate issued by an official vet within 10 days of travel, and for dogs a tapeworm treatment 24 to 120 hours before arrival. Pets from outside the EU must arrive as manifest cargo or with an approved airline on an approved route (Dublin Airport handles most), and are checked on arrival.

Settling in: community and daily life

The Bosnian community in Ireland is small but has been here a while, with families who arrived a generation ago alongside more recent workers, and it is centred on Dublin. Newcomers usually connect through the wider ex-Yugoslav circles, Facebook and WhatsApp groups, mosque and church communities, and football.

Coffee culture at home is long and social; in Ireland it is often a takeaway cup on the way somewhere, and the long evening sits happen in the pub instead. Rent is a much bigger share of income, groceries and restaurants cost more, and payments are mostly by card. Winters are milder but darker, and you drive on the left.

There are no regular direct flights between Dublin and Bosnia and Herzegovina, so getting home usually means one stop, most often via London, Frankfurt, Vienna, Istanbul or Warsaw; budget for the time as well as the fare.

First 30 days checklist

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • Register for your Irish Residence Permit within 90 days (300 euro); book the appointment the week you land because slots fill up.
  • Register with Revenue myAccount once you have a PPS number so your employer can tax you correctly.
  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.
  • Get a Leap card for public transport and book the driver theory test if you plan to drive.

★ Useful links

  • Immigration Service Delivery: visas and permissions
  • Employment permits
  • NARIC Ireland: qualification recognition
  • National Driver Licence Service
  • Revenue: moving to Ireland
  • Department of Agriculture: bringing your pet to Ireland
  • Health Insurance Authority

Some arrive for English-language study or university and stay for work; others follow family already here. Better wages and the chance to build something are the usual reasons. What surprises many Kosovars is how quiet Irish evenings are: shops and cafés close early, and the social life that fills the streets of Pristina is tucked away inside pubs.

Double taxation agreementYes
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Yes. Kosovar citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Kosovo, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.

Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Moving money from the Moldovan leu into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

The Turkish community in Ireland is medium-sized and growing, concentrated in Dublin with lively pockets in Cork and Galway around language schools and universities. Tea is still everywhere in Ireland, though it comes with milk rather than in a tulip glass, and the long social evening moves from the çay bahçesi to the pub. Rent is a much heavier burden than in most Turkish cities, groceries and eating out cost more, and payments are almost all by card. Winters are mild but dark and wet, and you drive on the left.

articles.note: D visa and a permit, no licence exchange, no tax treaty, no pension agreement.

articles.previewHtml:
Algeria sends a small but growing number of people to Ireland, most often for postgraduate study, research posts and jobs in engineering, IT, pharma and healthcare, with others arriving for English-language courses or to join family. Ireland's appeal is the combination of an English-speaking EU country with a large tech and pharma base, and some come via France, where they first studied or worked. The surprise for most Algerians is the daylight: long, bright summer evenings that last past ten, and winter afternoons that go dark before five.

Quick factsAlgeria to Ireland
Visa to enterYes, long stay D visa
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Algerian licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementNo
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Algerian citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Algeria, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

Algerians usually arrive with French and Arabic and a range of English, from fluent graduates to people still building confidence. Employers judge English in interview, while universities and professional registration bodies want formal results. Irish is on signs but not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Algerian qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Algeria is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Algerian licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Algerian licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Algeria have no double taxation agreement. For most people this matters less than it sounds: once you become Irish tax resident (183 days in a tax year, or 280 over two) and your job is here, Irish PAYE applies to your salary and your Algerian tax obligations usually end with your residence there. It matters if you keep Algerian income, such as rent or a business, which could be taxed in both countries; Revenue may grant unilateral relief for foreign tax paid, and a tax adviser is worth it in that case. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number.

There is no social security agreement between Ireland and Algeria, so the two records stand alone. You need at least 520 paid PRSI contributions (ten years) to qualify for any Irish State Pension (Contributory), and the full rate takes 40 years of contributions. Check whether your Algerian state pension can be paid to you in Ireland, and whether you can keep contributing voluntarily from abroad.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the Algerian dinar into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary. Algeria has exchange controls, so check what you are allowed to take out and the paperwork needed before you leave, and bring evidence of the source of funds for the Irish bank.

Healthcare

Ireland has a public system run by the HSE, but it is not free at the point of use. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods arriving from Algeria are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year. A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from Algeria rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.

Algeria is an unlisted country under the EU pet rules, which adds a blood test. Your dog, cat or ferret needs a microchip, then a rabies vaccination, then a rabies antibody titre test at least 30 days after the vaccination at an EU approved laboratory, and then a three month wait from the date of the blood sample before travel. Add an EU animal health certificate issued within 10 days of travel and, for dogs, a tapeworm treatment 24 to 120 hours before arrival. Pets must arrive as manifest cargo or with an approved airline on an approved route (Dublin Airport handles most). Start the process at least four months before you fly.

Settling in: community and daily life

The Algerian community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, concentrated in Dublin with a few families in Cork and Galway around the universities and hospitals. Newcomers tend to find each other through mosque communities, the wider Maghrebi and Francophone circles, university societies, and Facebook and WhatsApp groups.

Fresh bread, produce and a hot midday meal are harder to come by; Irish lunches are quick sandwiches and the main meal is in the evening. Rent takes a large share of income, groceries cost more, and everything is paid by card. Winters are mild but grey, halal food needs some seeking out beyond the cities, and driving is on the left.

There are no regular direct flights between Dublin and Algeria, so getting home usually means one stop, most often via London, Paris, Istanbul, Doha or Dubai; budget for the time as well as the fare.

First 30 days checklist

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • Register for your Irish Residence Permit within 90 days (300 euro); book the appointment the week you land because slots fill up.
  • Register with Revenue myAccount once you have a PPS number so your employer can tax you correctly.
  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.
  • Get a Leap card for public transport and book the driver theory test if you plan to drive.
  • If a pet is following later, get its rabies blood test done now so the three month clock is running.

What surprises many Egyptians is the pace of life: everything closes early, the streets are quiet by evening, and the Cairo habit of a late dinner out at midnight simply has no equivalent.

Double taxation agreementYes
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Yes. Egyptian citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Egypt, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Iran, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

Iranians who come through universities and tech usually have strong English, especially in writing, and employers judge fluency in interview rather than by certificate. Universities and professional registration bodies do ask for formal scores. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Iranian qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Iran is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Iranian licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Iranian licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Ireland and Iran have no double taxation agreement. For most people this matters less than it sounds: once you become Irish tax resident (183 days in a tax year, or 280 over two) and your job is here, Irish PAYE applies to your salary and your Iranian tax obligations usually end with your residence there. It matters if you keep Iranian income, such as rent or a business, which could be taxed in both countries; Revenue may grant unilateral relief for foreign tax paid, and a tax adviser is worth it in that case.
