articles.previewHtml:
Kuwait has a large expatriate workforce, so people moving from Kuwait to Ireland are usually Indian, Egyptian, Filipino, Pakistani or Lebanese professionals who have spent years in the Gulf and want a permanent home, along with Kuwaiti students heading to Irish universities, especially for medicine and engineering. Healthcare, tech, finance and construction are the typical sectors. The surprise for anyone arriving from Kuwait is how much of Irish life happens outdoors despite the weather: walking, cycling and standing outside pubs in the rain.

Quick factsKuwait to Ireland
Visa to enterYes, long stay D visa
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Kuwaiti licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementYes
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Kuwaiti citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Kuwait, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

English is the working language in Kuwait, so most arrivals speak it fluently, though Irish accents and slang take adjusting to. Employers rarely ask for a certificate, but universities and professional registration bodies do, even for fluent speakers. Irish is on signs but not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Kuwaiti qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Kuwait is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Kuwaiti licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Kuwaiti licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Kuwait have a double taxation agreement, so income taxed in one country is generally credited in the other and the treaty decides which country taxes what. You become Irish tax resident after 183 days in a tax year (or 280 days over two years), and from then Ireland taxes your worldwide income, with credit for Kuwaiti tax under the treaty. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number so your employer taxes you correctly, and tell the Kuwaiti tax authority that you are leaving.

There is no social security agreement between Ireland and Kuwait, so the two records stand alone. You need at least 520 paid PRSI contributions (ten years) to qualify for any Irish State Pension (Contributory), and the full rate takes 40 years of contributions. Check whether your Kuwaiti state pension can be paid to you in Ireland, and whether you can keep contributing voluntarily from abroad.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the Kuwaiti dinar into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Healthcare

Ireland has a public system run by the HSE, but it is not free at the point of use. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods arriving from Kuwait are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year. A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from Kuwait rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.

Kuwait is an unlisted country under the EU pet rules, which adds a blood test. Your dog, cat or ferret needs a microchip, then a rabies vaccination, then a rabies antibody titre test at least 30 days after the vaccination at an EU approved laboratory, and then a three month wait from the date of the blood sample before travel. Add an EU animal health certificate issued within 10 days of travel and, for dogs, a tapeworm treatment 24 to 120 hours before arrival. Pets must arrive as manifest cargo or with an approved airline on an approved route (Dublin Airport handles most). Start the process at least four months before you fly.

Settling in: community and daily life

The Kuwaiti community in Ireland is very small, mostly students and medical graduates in Dublin, while the broader group of people who have lived in Kuwait is larger and spread across the cities. Newcomers connect through university societies, mosque communities, Gulf alumni networks and WhatsApp groups of former colleagues.

Life in Kuwait runs on cars, air conditioning and late nights; in Ireland you walk more, dress in layers and find shops closing early. Petrol and domestic help are expensive rather than cheap, groceries cost more, and payments are by card. Weekends are Saturday and Sunday, and driving is on the left.

There are no regular direct flights between Dublin and Kuwait, so getting home usually means one stop, most often via London, Paris, Istanbul, Doha or Dubai; budget for the time as well as the fare.

First 30 days checklist

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • Register for your Irish Residence Permit within 90 days (300 euro); book the appointment the week you land because slots fill up.
  • Register with Revenue myAccount once you have a PPS number so your employer can tax you correctly.
  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.
  • Get a Leap card for public transport and book the driver theory test if you plan to drive.
  • If a pet is following later, get its rabies blood test done now so the three month clock is running.

  • National Driver Licence Service

  • Health Insurance Authority

You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Oman is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Omani licence for an Irish one. articles.previewHtml:
The UAE has an expatriate majority, so most people moving from the UAE to Ireland are Indian, Pakistani, Filipino, British, Egyptian or Lebanese professionals who spent years in Dubai or Abu Dhabi and now want a permanent home, better work-life balance and schooling for children, along with Emirati students heading to Irish universities. Healthcare, tech, finance, aviation and construction are the typical sectors. What surprises most arrivals from the Emirates is how small and informal Ireland feels: no towers, few malls, a boss who makes their own tea, and everyone walking in the rain.

Quick factsThe UAE to Ireland
Visa to enterNo, up to 90 days
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Emirati licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementYes
Social security agreementNo
PetsListed country, no blood test

Do you need a visa?

Emirati citizens are not visa required, so you can enter Ireland for up to 90 days without applying for anything. Staying longer is a different matter: you need an immigration permission before the 90 days run out, and you cannot turn a visit into a job from inside the country except through a handful of schemes. Get the permit or the college place sorted first, then travel. Ireland has added visa requirements for several countries since 2022, so check the current list on irishimmigration.ie before you book.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.
  • Stamp 0 for retirees and people of independent means, with income of around 50,000 euro a year per person and private medical insurance, and no right to work.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

English is the working language of the UAE, so most arrivals speak it fluently, though Irish accents and slang take adjusting to. Employers rarely ask for a certificate, but universities and professional registration bodies do, even for fluent speakers. Irish is on signs, not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Emirati qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

The UAE is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Emirati licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Emirati licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and the UAE have a double taxation agreement, so income taxed in one country is generally credited in the other and the treaty decides which country taxes what. You become Irish tax resident after 183 days in a tax year (or 280 days over two years), and from then Ireland taxes your worldwide income, with credit for Emirati tax under the treaty. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number so your employer taxes you correctly, and tell the Emirati tax authority that you are leaving.

There is no social security agreement between Ireland and the UAE, so the two records stand alone. You need at least 520 paid PRSI contributions (ten years) to qualify for any Irish State Pension (Contributory), and the full rate takes 40 years of contributions. Check whether your Emirati state pension can be paid to you in Ireland, and whether you can keep contributing voluntarily from abroad.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the UAE dirham into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Healthcare

Ireland has a public system run by the HSE, but it is not free at the point of use. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods arriving from the UAE are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year. A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from the UAE rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.

The UAE is a listed country under the EU pet rules, so no rabies blood test is needed. Your dog, cat or ferret needs a microchip, a rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel, an EU animal health certificate issued by an official vet within 10 days of travel, and for dogs a tapeworm treatment 24 to 120 hours before arrival. Pets from outside the EU must arrive as manifest cargo or with an approved airline on an approved route (Dublin Airport handles most), and are checked on arrival.

Settling in: community and daily life

The Emirati community in Ireland is tiny and mostly students, but the group of people who once lived in the UAE is large and spread across Dublin, Cork and Galway. Newcomers connect through former Dubai colleagues on WhatsApp, university societies, mosque communities, Indian and Filipino associations, and Gulf alumni networks.

Dubai's cars, delivery apps and air conditioning give way to walking, layers and shops that close early. Petrol, taxis and domestic help are expensive rather than cheap, groceries cost more, and everything is paid by card with light tipping. Weekends are Saturday and Sunday, and driving is on the left.

Getting home is straightforward: there are direct flights between Dublin and the UAE.

First 30 days checklist

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • Register for your Irish Residence Permit within 90 days (300 euro); book the appointment the week you land because slots fill up.
  • Register with Revenue myAccount once you have a PPS number so your employer can tax you correctly.
  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.
  • Get a Leap card for public transport and book the driver theory test if you plan to drive.

  • Department of Agriculture: bringing your pet to Ireland
  • Health Insurance Authority

Botswana is a small country with a well-educated, English-speaking workforce, and the people who move to Ireland are usually nurses and other healthcare staff, students on postgraduate courses, accountants, and engineers who see Ireland as a friendly first step into Europe. Family ties and a spouse's job bring others. Because Botswana runs on English and a Commonwealth-style institutional culture, the working world feels familiar quickly. The thing that surprises most Batswana is the rain: not its volume so much as its persistence, with a fine drizzle that can last for days and sunlight that feels rationed in winter.

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Botswanan citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Botswana, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

English is an official language of Botswana, so most arrivals are fluent and employers treat you accordingly. Expect a slightly different vocabulary, fast Irish accents that vary by county, and plenty of understatement. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Botswanan qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Botswana is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Botswanan licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Botswanan licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Botswana have a double taxation agreement, so income taxed in one country is generally credited in the other and the treaty decides which country taxes what. You become Irish tax resident after 183 days in a tax year (or 280 days over two years), and from then Ireland taxes your worldwide income, with credit for Botswanan tax under the treaty. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number so your employer taxes you correctly, and tell the Botswanan tax authority that you are leaving.

There is no social security agreement between Ireland and Botswana, so the two records stand alone. You need at least 520 paid PRSI contributions (ten years) to qualify for any Irish State Pension (Contributory), and the full rate takes 40 years of contributions. Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the pula into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

The Burundian community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, mostly in Dublin with families in other towns. The Central African Republic sends only a handful of people to Ireland, and they usually come for study, to join family, or through work with international organisations, healthcare and care roles, or church networks. Some arrive after years in France or Cameroon and want the chance to build an English-speaking career. Because the numbers are so small, newcomers often become the first Central African their Irish neighbours have met. The thing that surprises most is how safe and predictable daily life feels, and how much of it is organised around appointments, timetables and the weather forecast.

Visa to enterYes, long stay D visa
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Central African licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementNo
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Central African citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers the Central African Republic, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. The Central African Republic is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Central African licence for an Irish one. Chad is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Chadian licence for an Irish one. Moving money from the Central African CFA franc into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Equatorial Guinea sends only a very small number of people to Ireland, most often postgraduate students, engineers with oil and gas experience, healthcare workers, and people joining family already in Europe. Many have first lived in Spain and come to Ireland for English-language study or to build a career in an English-speaking EU country. With so few Equatoguineans around, newcomers tend to find their way into wider Spanish-speaking and African networks. What surprises most is the cost and competitiveness of renting and how quickly you need to move when a decent room comes up.

Quick factsEquatorial Guinea to Ireland
Visa to enterYes, long stay D visa
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Equatoguinean licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementNo
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Equatoguinean citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Equatorial Guinea, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

Spanish is the everyday language for most Equatoguineans, so confident English is the main preparation for interviews and a concise CV. Employers rarely ask for IELTS, but universities and registration bodies often do. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Equatoguinean qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Equatorial Guinea is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Equatoguinean licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Equatoguinean licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Equatorial Guinea have no double taxation agreement. For most people this matters less than it sounds: once you become Irish tax resident (183 days in a tax year, or 280 over two) and your job is here, Irish PAYE applies to your salary and your Equatoguinean tax obligations usually end with your residence there. Moving money from the Central African CFA franc into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Goods arriving from Equatorial Guinea are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year. A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from Equatorial Guinea rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.

Equatorial Guinea is an unlisted country under the EU pet rules, which adds a blood test. Your dog, cat or ferret needs a microchip, then a rabies vaccination, then a rabies antibody titre test at least 30 days after the vaccination at an EU approved laboratory, and then a three month wait from the date of the blood sample before travel. Settling in: community and daily life

There is no established Equatoguinean community in Ireland, just a handful of students and professionals mostly in Dublin. Newcomers usually connect through Spanish-speaking groups, wider African associations, churches, university international offices and WhatsApp groups rather than through a dedicated association.

The cool, wet weather and short winter days are a marked change from Malabo, though summer evenings stay bright late. Renting is expensive and paperwork-heavy. Groceries cost more than at home, eating out is dearer still, cards are used for almost everything, and much of social life revolves around the pub.

There are no regular direct flights between Dublin and Equatorial Guinea, so getting home usually means one stop, most often via London, Paris, Amsterdam, Istanbul, Addis Ababa, Doha or Dubai; budget for the time as well as the fare.

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • Register for your Irish Residence Permit within 90 days (300 euro); book the appointment the week you land because slots fill up.

  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.

  • Get a Leap card for public transport and book the driver theory test if you plan to drive.
  • If a pet is following later, get its rabies blood test done now so the three month clock is running.

English is an official language of Eswatini, so most arrivals are fluent and are treated as such by employers. Expect fast, varied Irish accents and plenty of understatement and slang. Irish appears on road signs and public buildings but is not needed for daily life.

Ireland has a public system run by the HSE, but it is not free at the point of use. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

English is an official language of Kenya and most arrivals are fluent, so employers treat you accordingly. Expect fast Irish accents that vary by county, plenty of slang and understatement, and a few different everyday words. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Kenya is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Kenyan licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Kenyan licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the Kenyan shilling into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

articles.previewHtml:
Malawi sends a small but steady number of people to Ireland, most often nurses and other healthcare workers, postgraduate students, teachers, accountants and people joining family. Ireland's long development links with Malawi mean many Irish people have worked or volunteered there, which often makes for warm first conversations. English is the language of education at home, so Malawians settle into Irish hospitals and universities fairly quickly. What surprises newcomers most is the Irish winter: short, grey days and persistent drizzle after Malawi's bright, warm climate and long lakeside evenings.

Quick factsMalawi to Ireland
Visa to enterNo, up to 90 days
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Malawian licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementNo
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Do you need a visa?

Malawian citizens are not visa required, so you can enter Ireland for up to 90 days without applying for anything. Staying longer is a different matter: you need an immigration permission before the 90 days run out, and you cannot turn a visit into a job from inside the country except through a handful of schemes. Get the permit or the college place sorted first, then travel. Ireland has added visa requirements for several countries since 2022, so check the current list on irishimmigration.ie before you book.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.
  • Stamp 0 for retirees and people of independent means, with income of around 50,000 euro a year per person and private medical insurance, and no right to work.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

English is an official language of Malawi and most arrivals are fluent, so employers treat you accordingly. Expect fast Irish accents that vary sharply by county and plenty of slang and understatement. Irish appears on signs and public buildings but is not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Malawian qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Malawi is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Malawian licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Malawian licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Malawi have no double taxation agreement. For most people this matters less than it sounds: once you become Irish tax resident (183 days in a tax year, or 280 over two) and your job is here, Irish PAYE applies to your salary and your Malawian tax obligations usually end with your residence there. It matters if you keep Malawian income, such as rent or a business, which could be taxed in both countries; Revenue may grant unilateral relief for foreign tax paid, and a tax adviser is worth it in that case. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number.

There is no social security agreement between Ireland and Malawi, so the two records stand alone. You need at least 520 paid PRSI contributions (ten years) to qualify for any Irish State Pension (Contributory), and the full rate takes 40 years of contributions. Check whether your Malawian state pension can be paid to you in Ireland, and whether you can keep contributing voluntarily from abroad.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the kwacha into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Healthcare

Ireland has a public system run by the HSE, but it is not free at the point of use. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods arriving from Malawi are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year. A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from Malawi rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.

Malawi is an unlisted country under the EU pet rules, which adds a blood test. Your dog, cat or ferret needs a microchip, then a rabies vaccination, then a rabies antibody titre test at least 30 days after the vaccination at an EU approved laboratory, and then a three month wait from the date of the blood sample before travel. Add an EU animal health certificate issued within 10 days of travel and, for dogs, a tapeworm treatment 24 to 120 hours before arrival. Pets must arrive as manifest cargo or with an approved airline on an approved route (Dublin Airport handles most). Start the process at least four months before you fly.

Settling in: community and daily life

The Malawian community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, spread between Dublin, Cork, Limerick and hospital towns. Newcomers usually find each other through church congregations, wider Southern African groups, and WhatsApp and Facebook groups, with occasional gatherings around national celebrations.

Driving on the left is familiar, but Irish roads are narrower and public transport outside Dublin is limited. Renting is the big adjustment, with competitive viewings and references expected. Groceries in the big chains are manageable, eating out costs more than in Lilongwe or Blantyre, and cards are used almost everywhere.

There are no regular direct flights between Dublin and Malawi, so getting home usually means one stop, most often via London, Paris, Amsterdam, Istanbul, Addis Ababa, Doha or Dubai; budget for the time as well as the fare.

First 30 days checklist

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • Register for your Irish Residence Permit within 90 days (300 euro); book the appointment the week you land because slots fill up.
  • Register with Revenue myAccount once you have a PPS number so your employer can tax you correctly.
  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.
  • Get a Leap card for public transport and book the driver theory test if you plan to drive.
  • If a pet is following later, get its rabies blood test done now so the three month clock is running.

★ Useful links

  • Immigration Service Delivery: visas and permissions
  • Employment permits
  • NARIC Ireland: qualification recognition
  • National Driver Licence Service
  • Revenue: moving to Ireland
  • Department of Agriculture: bringing your pet to Ireland
  • Health Insurance Authority

Mauritius sends a steady stream of people to Ireland, most often nurses and healthcare workers, hospitality and hotel staff, accountants and finance professionals, IT staff and postgraduate students. Mauritians grow up switching between English, French and Creole, which makes them well suited to Irish hospitals, hotels and the international companies in Dublin, and family ties bring others over time. What surprises Mauritian newcomers most is the winter: not so much the temperature as the short, grey days and the way the sea is something to look at rather than swim in for most of the year.

Quick factsMauritius to IrelandVisa to enterNo, up to 90 daysPermission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRPMauritian licence exchangeableNoDouble taxation agreementNoSocial security agreementNoPetsListed country, no blood test

Do you need a visa?

Mauritian citizens are not visa required, so you can enter Ireland for up to 90 days without applying for anything. Staying longer is a different matter: you need an immigration permission before the 90 days run out, and you cannot turn a visit into a job from inside the country except through a handful of schemes. Get the permit or the college place sorted first, then travel. Ireland has added visa requirements for several countries since 2022, so check the current list on irishimmigration.ie before you book.

Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.Stamp 0 for retirees and people of independent means, with income of around 50,000 euro a year per person and private medical insurance, and no right to work.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

Most Mauritians arrive fluent in English, though often as a second working language after French and Creole, so a confident interview manner helps. Employers rarely ask for IELTS, but registration bodies and universities often do. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Mauritian qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Mauritius is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Mauritian licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Mauritian licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Mauritius have no double taxation agreement. For most people this matters less than it sounds: once you become Irish tax resident (183 days in a tax year, or 280 over two) and your job is here, Irish PAYE applies to your salary and your Mauritian tax obligations usually end with your residence there. It matters if you keep Mauritian income, such as rent or a business, which could be taxed in both countries; Revenue may grant unilateral relief for foreign tax paid, and a tax adviser is worth it in that case. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number.

There is no social security agreement between Ireland and Mauritius, so the two records stand alone. You need at least 520 paid PRSI contributions (ten years) to qualify for any Irish State Pension (Contributory), and the full rate takes 40 years of contributions. Check whether your Mauritian state pension can be paid to you in Ireland, and whether you can keep contributing voluntarily from abroad.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the Mauritian rupee into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Healthcare

Ireland has a public system run by the HSE, but it is not free at the point of use. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Goods arriving from Mauritius are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year. articles.previewHtml:
Rwanda sends a small but steady number of people to Ireland, most often for postgraduate study, healthcare work and roles in development organisations and tech. Kigali's growing start-up and public-sector scene means many arrivals already have professional experience and come to add a master's degree or a few years abroad before deciding where to settle. Others join family already here or come through church and NGO links that connect the two countries. What surprises most Rwandans first is the cold, damp wind rather than the temperature itself.

Quick factsRwanda to Ireland
Visa to enterYes, long stay D visa
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Rwandan licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementNo
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Rwandan citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Rwanda, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

Most Rwandans arrive with strong English from school and work, often alongside French and Kinyarwanda, so interviews are rarely a problem. Irish employers seldom ask for IELTS, though universities and professional registration bodies may. Irish appears on signs but you will not need it.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Rwandan qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Rwanda is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Rwandan licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Rwandan licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Rwanda have no double taxation agreement. For most people this matters less than it sounds: once you become Irish tax resident (183 days in a tax year, or 280 over two) and your job is here, Irish PAYE applies to your salary and your Rwandan tax obligations usually end with your residence there. It matters if you keep Rwandan income, such as rent or a business, which could be taxed in both countries; Revenue may grant unilateral relief for foreign tax paid, and a tax adviser is worth it in that case. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number.

Moving money from the Rwandan franc into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Goods arriving from Rwanda are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year. A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from Rwanda rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.

Rwanda is an unlisted country under the EU pet rules, which adds a blood test. Your dog, cat or ferret needs a microchip, then a rabies vaccination, then a rabies antibody titre test at least 30 days after the vaccination at an EU approved laboratory, and then a three month wait from the date of the blood sample before travel. Pets must arrive as manifest cargo or with an approved airline on an approved route (Dublin Airport handles most). Start the process at least four months before you fly.

Settling in: community and daily life

The Rwandan community in Ireland is small and fairly recent, concentrated in Dublin with a scattering of students and health workers in Cork, Galway and Limerick. Newcomers usually find each other through university African societies, church congregations, embassy-linked commemoration and cultural events, and WhatsApp groups passed on by a friend of a friend.

Kigali's mild, sunny highland climate and its early, predictable sunsets give way to short grey winter days and long bright summer evenings. Renting is more formal and competitive than at home, groceries and eating out cost more, and you will drive on the left. Card and contactless payments dominate, and mobile money as you know it barely exists.

There are no regular direct flights between Dublin and Rwanda, so getting home usually means one stop, most often via London, Paris, Amsterdam, Istanbul, Addis Ababa, Doha or Dubai; budget for the time as well as the fare.

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • Register for your Irish Residence Permit within 90 days (300 euro); book the appointment the week you land because slots fill up.

  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.
  • Get a Leap card for public transport and book the driver theory test if you plan to drive.
  • If a pet is following later, get its rabies blood test done now so the three month clock is running.

Senegal is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Senegalese licence for an Irish one. Moving money from the West African CFA franc into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from Senegal rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.

Sudan has sent doctors, engineers, pharmacists and academics abroad for generations, and Ireland has become a real destination for Sudanese healthcare workers, postgraduate students and families, often via the Gulf, Egypt or the UK. Hospitals across the country employ Sudanese doctors and nurses, while universities in Dublin, Cork and Galway attract researchers in medicine, engineering and agriculture. Instability at home has also brought people joining relatives already settled here. What surprises most Sudanese first is how informal and first-name Irish workplaces are, even in hospitals, compared with the hierarchy they are used to.

Togo is a small and recent source of arrivals to Ireland, mostly students, healthcare and care workers, hospitality staff and young professionals in tech and finance, many of whom lived in France or Germany first. Lomé's francophone graduates often choose Ireland precisely to work in English inside the EU, and some come through family or church connections. Others arrive after study in Ghana or Nigeria with English already in hand. What surprises most Togolese first is the cost of a simple meal out and how much cooking at home becomes part of life.

Visa to enterYes, long stay D visa
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Togolese licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementNo
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Togolese citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Togo, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Uganda has deep links with Ireland through long-standing Irish aid programmes, missionaries and university partnerships, and Ugandans come for postgraduate study, nursing and care work, medicine, tech and NGO roles, and to join family already here. Kampala's large English-speaking graduate population makes Ireland a natural next step, especially for health professionals and public-health researchers. Some arrive via the UK, where Ugandan communities are larger. What surprises most Ugandans first is the silence: how quiet neighbourhoods are at night and how few people are out on the street after dark.

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Ugandan citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Uganda, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

English is Uganda's official language and most arrivals speak it fluently, so interviews are rarely a problem beyond adjusting to Irish accents and understatement. Employers do not usually ask for IELTS, though registration bodies and universities may. Irish is on signs but not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Ugandan qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Uganda is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Ugandan licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Ugandan licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Ireland and Uganda have no double taxation agreement. For most people this matters less than it sounds: once you become Irish tax resident (183 days in a tax year, or 280 over two) and your job is here, Irish PAYE applies to your salary and your Ugandan tax obligations usually end with your residence there. It matters if you keep Ugandan income, such as rent or a business, which could be taxed in both countries; Revenue may grant unilateral relief for foreign tax paid, and a tax adviser is worth it in that case. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the Ugandan shilling into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Goods arriving from Uganda are imports from outside the EU. A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from Uganda rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.
