Check whether your Papua New Guinean state pension can be paid to you in Ireland, and whether you can keep contributing voluntarily from abroad.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the kina into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Ireland has a public system run by the HSE, but it is not free at the point of use. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Goods arriving from Papua New Guinea are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year. A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from Papua New Guinea rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.

Papua New Guinea is an unlisted country under the EU pet rules, which adds a blood test. Your dog, cat or ferret needs a microchip, then a rabies vaccination, then a rabies antibody titre test at least 30 days after the vaccination at an EU approved laboratory, and then a three month wait from the date of the blood sample before travel. Add an EU animal health certificate issued within 10 days of travel and, for dogs, a tapeworm treatment 24 to 120 hours before arrival. Pets must arrive as manifest cargo or with an approved airline on an approved route (Dublin Airport handles most). Start the process at least four months before you fly.

Settling in: community and daily life

There is no established Papua New Guinean community in Ireland, just a scattering of students, health workers and clergy, mostly in Dublin and Maynooth. Newcomers usually find connection through Catholic parishes and religious orders with PNG links, university international societies, and the wider Pacific Islander and Australian circles in Ireland.

The climate is the biggest daily adjustment: cool, wet and windy most of the year, with heating rather than air conditioning as the household concern, and winter days that end mid-afternoon. Groceries cost more and fresh tropical produce is limited, so Asian and African shops become useful. Card payments dominate, and driving is on the left as at home.

There are no regular direct flights between Dublin and Papua New Guinea, so getting home usually means one stop, most often via Dubai, Doha, Singapore or Los Angeles; budget for the time as well as the fare.

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • Register for your Irish Residence Permit within 90 days (300 euro); book the appointment the week you land because slots fill up.
  • Register with Revenue myAccount once you have a PPS number so your employer can tax you correctly.
  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.
  • Get a Leap card for public transport and book the driver theory test if you plan to drive.
  • If a pet is following later, get its rabies blood test done now so the three month clock is running.

Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. What surprises Colombians most is how reserved Irish people can seem at first and how quickly that reserve dissolves after a single evening in the pub.

articles.description: Costa Rica sends a modest but steady group to Ireland, many of them young professionals with experience in the tech, customer support and medtech…
articles.previewHtml:
Costa Rica sends a modest but steady group to Ireland, many of them young professionals with experience in the tech, customer support and medtech operations that both countries host for the same multinationals, along with students at Irish universities and language schools. Others come to join Irish partners met while travelling, or simply for a few years of European life. What surprises Costa Ricans most is the absence of a proper rainy season: instead of afternoon downpours followed by sun, Ireland offers light rain at any hour, any month, without warning.

Quick factsCosta Rica to Ireland
Visa to enterNo, up to 90 days
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Costa Rican licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementNo
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Do you need a visa?

Costa Rican citizens are not visa required, so you can enter Ireland for up to 90 days without applying for anything. Staying longer is a different matter: you need an immigration permission before the 90 days run out, and you cannot turn a visit into a job from inside the country except through a handful of schemes. Get the permit or the college place sorted first, then travel. Ireland has added visa requirements for several countries since 2022, so check the current list on irishimmigration.ie before you book.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.
  • Stamp 0 for retirees and people of independent means, with income of around 50,000 euro a year per person and private medical insurance, and no right to work.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

Many Costa Ricans arrive with good English from school, tourism or multinational work, so the adjustment is to Irish accents and slang; employers interview rather than ask for IELTS, though universities and professional bodies may. Irish is on signs but not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Costa Rican qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Costa Rica is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Costa Rican licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Costa Rican licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Costa Rica have no double taxation agreement. For most people this matters less than it sounds: once you become Irish tax resident (183 days in a tax year, or 280 over two) and your job is here, Irish PAYE applies to your salary and your Costa Rican tax obligations usually end with your residence there. It matters if you keep Costa Rican income, such as rent or a business, which could be taxed in both countries; Revenue may grant unilateral relief for foreign tax paid, and a tax adviser is worth it in that case. Register with Revenue through myAccount as soon as you have a PPS number.

There is no social security agreement between Ireland and Costa Rica, so the two records stand alone. You need at least 520 paid PRSI contributions (ten years) to qualify for any Irish State Pension (Contributory), and the full rate takes 40 years of contributions. Check whether your Costa Rican state pension can be paid to you in Ireland, and whether you can keep contributing voluntarily from abroad.

Your credit history does not follow you. Irish lenders only see the Central Credit Register, so expect to build a record from scratch before a mortgage or car loan. Moving money from the colón into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Healthcare

Ireland has a public system run by the HSE, but it is not free at the point of use. Once you are ordinarily resident (living in Ireland or intending to for at least a year) you use public hospitals as a public patient, and inpatient charges were abolished in April 2023. A GP visit costs roughly 50 to 70 euro unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card on income grounds (children under 8 get GP visits free), and prescriptions are paid for up to a monthly cap under the Drugs Payment Scheme. Emergency departments charge 100 euro without a GP referral. Students, Stamp 0 holders and most visa applicants must show private medical insurance, so many people arrive with a policy already.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods arriving from Costa Rica are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year. A car qualifies for VRT relief on the same terms, but shipping a car from Costa Rica rarely makes sense once freight, registration and Irish insurance are added up.

Costa Rica is an unlisted country under the EU pet rules, which adds a blood test. Your dog, cat or ferret needs a microchip, then a rabies vaccination, then a rabies antibody titre test at least 30 days after the vaccination at an EU approved laboratory, and then a three month wait from the date of the blood sample before travel. Add an EU animal health certificate issued within 10 days of travel and, for dogs, a tapeworm treatment 24 to 120 hours before arrival. Pets must arrive as manifest cargo or with an approved airline on an approved route (Dublin Airport handles most). Start the process at least four months before you fly.

Settling in: community and daily life

The Costa Rican community in Ireland is small and recent, mostly in Dublin and often working for the same multinationals that have offices back home. Newcomers usually find each other through Central American and wider Latin American WhatsApp groups, football, Spanish-language Catholic parishes, and occasional gatherings organised through the embassy.

Daylight is the strangest change: long summer evenings and then winter darkness by late afternoon, rather than the even twelve-hour days of home. Rents are high, groceries cost more, and fresh fruit is more expensive and less varied. Tipping is light, cards are used for everything, and driving is on the left.

There are no regular direct flights between Dublin and Costa Rica, so getting home usually means one stop, most often via London, Madrid, Lisbon, Paris, Amsterdam or a North American hub; budget for the time as well as the fare.

First 30 days checklist

  • Apply for a PPS number through MyWelfare.ie with your passport and proof of Irish address.
  • Register for your Irish Residence Permit within 90 days (300 euro); book the appointment the week you land because slots fill up.
  • Register with Revenue myAccount once you have a PPS number so your employer can tax you correctly.
  • Open an Irish bank account; a utility bill, tenancy agreement or employer letter usually counts as proof of address.
  • Register with a GP and, if you want it, buy private health insurance within 9 months.
  • Get a Leap card for public transport and book the driver theory test if you plan to drive.
  • If a pet is following later, get its rabies blood test done now so the three month clock is running.

Social security agreementNo

For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Ecuador, or through its VFS partner where one is used. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. Many Ecuadorians arrive with intermediate English and use a language school plus part-time work to bring it up; employers hire on how you interview rather than a certificate, though universities and professional registration bodies may require IELTS. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Honduras sends a small number of people to Ireland, and the usual routes are English-language study, postgraduate courses at Irish universities, and work in hospitality, construction, healthcare and the customer support operations of multinationals, sometimes after time in Spain or the United States. Some come to join partners or family. What surprises Hondurans most is how safe and calm daily life feels, walking home late without a second thought, and how that calm comes with an early bedtime for the whole country.

Quick factsHonduras to Ireland
Visa to enterYes, long stay D visa
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Honduran licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementNo
Social security agreementNo
PetsUnlisted country, rabies blood test

Do you need a visa?

Yes. Honduran citizens are visa required, so you need an Irish visa before you travel and then an immigration permission to stay. For a move the visa is a long stay D visa, applied for online through AVATS and submitted with your passport and documents to the Irish embassy or visa office that covers Honduras, or through its VFS partner where one is used. Allow at least eight weeks. The visa gets you to the border; your permission to live here comes from the permit, course or family relationship behind it. You cannot enter on a short stay C visa and switch to a work permission from inside Ireland.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

Finding work and getting your qualifications recognised

English is often the main challenge for Honduran arrivals, and language school with part-time work is the common starting point; employers judge you in interview rather than by certificate, though universities and professional bodies may ask for IELTS. Irish is on signs but not needed.

Because most routes need a job offer first, the search happens from home. Irish CVs run to two pages, carry no photo and no date of birth, and lead with what you did rather than your job title. Most hiring runs through LinkedIn, IrishJobs, Jobs.ie and the employers' own sites; agencies are strong in tech, finance, pharma and healthcare, and employers used to sponsoring permits say so in the advert. Get your degree assessed by NARIC Ireland (free, through QQI) before you apply; it maps a Honduran qualification onto the Irish framework and employers recognise the letter. Regulated professions register with their own body: nurses with NMBI, doctors with the Medical Council, teachers with the Teaching Council, engineers with Engineers Ireland, and physiotherapists, radiographers and social workers with CORU. Those bodies, not employers, are the ones that ask for an English test.

Your driving licence

Honduras is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Honduran licence for an Irish one. You can drive on your Honduran licence for up to 12 months as a visitor, ideally with an International Driving Permit, but once you are resident you must go through the Irish process: pass the driver theory test, get a learner permit, complete Essential Driver Training and pass the driving test. The good news is that experienced foreign licence holders only need 6 EDT lessons instead of 12 and can skip the usual six month wait before the test. Learner permit holders must be accompanied by a full licence holder, which is the part that catches people out. Remember that Ireland drives on the left.

Tax, pensions and money

Ireland and Honduras have no double taxation agreement. For most people this matters less than it sounds: once you become Irish tax resident (183 days in a tax year, or 280 over two) and your job is here, Irish PAYE applies to your salary and your Honduran tax obligations usually end with your residence there. Moving money from the lempira into euro is cheapest through a specialist transfer provider rather than a bank; open the Irish account first, because you need an Irish IBAN to receive salary.

Around half the population holds private health insurance from VHI, Laya or Irish Life Health, mainly to shorten waiting lists. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Goods arriving from Honduras are imports from outside the EU. articles.previewHtml:
Trinidad and Tobago has a modest, long-running connection with Ireland, partly through medicine and universities and partly through the Catholic church and Irish teaching orders that once ran schools there. Trinidadians come here for medicine, nursing, engineering, finance and postgraduate study, often via Britain or Canada where the diaspora is larger. Energy sector experience travels well into Irish engineering and consulting. What surprises arrivals most is the cold, grey winter and the sheer length of a wet season that never seems to end.

Visa to enterNo, up to 90 days
Permission to stay beyond 90 daysYes, needs a permit or scheme, then an IRP
Trinidadian and Tobagonian licence exchangeableNo
Double taxation agreementNo
Social security agreementNo
PetsListed country, no blood test

Do you need a visa?

Trinidadian and Tobagonian citizens are not visa required, so you can enter Ireland for up to 90 days without applying for anything. Staying longer is a different matter: you need an immigration permission before the 90 days run out, and you cannot turn a visit into a job from inside the country except through a handful of schemes. Get the permit or the college place sorted first, then travel. Ireland has added visa requirements for several countries since 2022, so check the current list on irishimmigration.ie before you book.

  • Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Spouses and partners can join you and work on Stamp 1G without their own permit, and you can apply for Stamp 4 after two years.
  • General Employment Permit for most other jobs, minimum salary 36,605 euro from 1 March 2026, usually after the employer runs a labour market needs test. Healthcare assistants, home carers, chefs and construction trades come in on this permit.
  • Stamp 2 study permission for a degree or a recognised English language course, with the right to work 20 hours a week in term time (40 in the holidays). Graduates of Irish degrees get the Third Level Graduate Programme (Stamp 1G) to look for work for one to two years.
  • Family routes if you are joining an Irish citizen, an EU citizen exercising treaty rights, or a permit holder.
  • Stamp 0 for retirees and people of independent means, with income of around 50,000 euro a year per person and private medical insurance, and no right to work.

Whichever route you take, you must register for an Irish Residence Permit (300 euro) within 90 days of arriving: online in Dublin, or at the local Garda immigration office elsewhere. If you have an Irish born parent or grandparent, check the Foreign Births Register first, because once registered you are an Irish citizen and none of the above applies.

English is the official language of Trinidad and Tobago, so there is no language barrier, only accent and idiom in both directions; Irish colleagues will adjust to your rhythm and you to theirs quickly. Irish appears on signs but is not needed.

Trinidad and Tobago is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Trinidadian and Tobagonian licence for an Irish one. Critical Skills Employment Permit for jobs on the critical skills list (from 1 March 2026 the minimum salary is 40,904 euro, or 68,911 euro for other eligible roles). Many Uruguayans arrive with intermediate English and use a language school and a café job to bring it up fast; employers hire on how you interview rather than a certificate, though universities and professional bodies may require IELTS. Irish is on signs but not needed.

Uruguay is not on the NDLS list of recognised states, so you cannot swap a Uruguayan licence for an Irish one. If you are 35 or older, buy it within 9 months of arriving to avoid a Lifetime Community Rating loading. Register with a GP as soon as you have an address; practices in Dublin often have closed lists, so ask several.

Bringing your things and your pet

Goods arriving from Uruguay are imports from outside the EU. You can bring your household belongings free of duty and VAT under Transfer of Residence relief if you have lived outside the EU for at least 12 months and owned the goods for at least 6 months; your removals company files the declaration and you cannot sell the goods for a year.
